A bully is a person who uses their power, strength, or position to repeatedly hurt, frighten, humiliate, or control someone who is weaker or less able to defend themselves.

Two things are essential to understanding this word:

1. Repetition. A single unkind act does not make someone a bully. A bully makes a habit of targeting the same person, again and again. This is what separates a bully from someone who is simply rude on a bad day.

2. A power imbalance. A bully always has more power than their target. This power can come from many sources — being physically bigger, being more popular, being older, having a louder voice in a group, or holding a position of authority (like a boss or a team captain). The target feels helpless: they cannot easily fight back, escape, or get others to listen to them.

A bully does not have to be physically violent. Bullying takes many forms:

  • Physical: hitting, pushing, blocking someone's path, destroying their belongings, or making physical threats.
  • Verbal: name-calling, mocking, insulting, belittling, or publicly humiliating someone.
  • Social/relational: spreading rumors, turning a group against someone, deliberately excluding them, or sabotaging their friendships and reputation.
  • Cyber: doing any of the above through phones, social media, or the internet. The person doing this is called a cyberbully.

A "bully" is an umbrella term — it covers anyone who fits the pattern, regardless of which of these methods they use.

Bullying is not limited to children or schools. You will encounter this word used in many contexts:

  • A school bully or playground bully is the most familiar image — a child who repeatedly picks on, frightens, or dominates classmates. This is what most people picture first.
  • A workplace bully (also called an office bully) is an adult — often a manager, supervisor, or colleague — who demeans, undermines, threatens, or controls another person at work.
  • In politics and international affairs, a powerful nation, government, or leader that uses threats, force, or coercion to dominate weaker countries or people is also called a bully. Example: "The neighboring country has been acting like a regional bully, pressuring smaller nations into signing unfair agreements."

The word works in any context where someone with more power repeatedly abuses that power over someone with less.

Bullies act the way they do to gain something: a feeling of control, social status (looking "tough" or dominant), attention, or to mask their own deep insecurities and fears. Many bullies need an audience — they behave worse in front of others because the act is partly a performance designed to show the group who is in charge. When bystanders watch and do nothing, they unintentionally encourage the bully.

Calling someone "a bully" is a strong accusation. It is not like calling someone "rude" or "difficult." It implies a pattern of behavior — that this person deliberately and repeatedly targets someone who cannot protect themselves. It carries a moral judgment: a bully is seen as a coward who takes advantage of weakness, not as someone who is merely being careless or thoughtless.

Example sentences:

  • "Everyone in the class was afraid of Marcus — he was the school bully who made life miserable for the younger students."
  • "Her manager turned out to be a bully who shouted at employees and took credit for their work."
  • "Stop being a bully and let her speak."
  • "The international community condemned the larger country for acting like a bully toward its smaller neighbors."
A completely different, older meaning — still alive in two phrases

Here is something that surprises many learners: centuries ago, "bully" had a positive meaning. It meant something excellent, splendid, or admirable, and could also refer to a dear friend or companion. This sense is now almost entirely gone from everyday English, but it survives in two specific expressions you will encounter:

"Bully for you!"
This phrase means "Good for you!" or "Well done!" — drawing on the old, positive meaning of bully. However, today it is used almost exclusively in a sarcastic tone, implying that the speaker is decidedly unimpressed by what you've done. If someone announces something with great pride and another person flatly responds, "Oh, bully for you," they are being dismissive, not genuinely congratulatory. Context and tone decide which meaning is intended, but sarcasm is by far the more common modern use.

"Bully pulpit"
This phrase was coined by U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt in the early 1900s. A bully pulpit refers to a highly visible public platform or position of authority that gives its holder an exceptional opportunity to speak out, advocate for causes, and shape public opinion. Roosevelt used "bully" in its old sense of "excellent" or "first-rate" — meaning the presidency was an excellent platform for influencing people. Today, journalists, politicians, and commentators use this phrase regularly. Example: "The presidency gives its holder a bully pulpit to push for social change." This has nothing to do with intimidation — it is entirely about the power of a platform.

These are uncommon, but a truly complete understanding of the word means knowing they exist:

Bully (in field hockey): In the sport of field hockey, a "bully" is a method of restarting play. Two opposing players alternately tap the ground and each other's sticks three times before competing for the ball. If you ever read about field hockey, you may see phrases like "the game was restarted with a bully." This meaning is entirely unrelated to intimidation.

Bully beef: An old British informal term for canned corned beef (preserved, salted beef). It appears in historical texts, World War-era diaries, and old literature. This meaning is essentially obsolete in modern everyday speech, but you may come across it in historical reading.

The noun "bully" has the following distinct senses:

The dominant modern meaning (what people almost always mean): A person who repeatedly uses power, strength, or position to intimidate, harm, humiliate, or control someone weaker. This applies to children, adults, individuals, institutions, and nations alike.

A surviving archaic meaning: Something excellent or admirable — preserved today only in the fixed phrases "bully for you!" (usually sarcastic) and "bully pulpit" (a powerful platform for advocacy).

Rare, specialized meanings: A restart method in field hockey; an old British word for canned beef — both essentially limited to their own specific contexts.

When you encounter the word in daily life — in news, in conversation, in literature — the first meaning is what is meant in nearly every case. The others are interesting layers that give you the full depth of this word across time and usage.
